title: How do we expand (6x + 5) squared in two ways?
description: The square of six x plus five is expanded with the identity and again with the distributive property. Then we find when the square of a sum is greater than the two squares added. Keeko doubts that squaring each term is enough.
teaching_notes: One idea: the square of a sum is the two squares plus twice the first times the second. Watch for students who square each term and add, leaving out the middle term.

source: Expand (6x + 5)² with the identity and with the distributive property, and say when (a + b)² is greater than a² + b².
video_script.why: The child has cut a square of side sixty five into two squares and two rectangles. Here the same four parts are written with letters.
video_script.substitution: Put the first and second terms in the identity, expand by the distributive property to confirm, then compare the square of a sum with the two squares.
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko squares each term and adds, getting thirty six x squared plus twenty five. With x as one, the question gives one hundred twenty one but that answer gives only sixty one.
video_script.payoff_line: The extra part is twice the first times the second

final_answer.value: 36x² + 60x + 25; (a + b)² is greater than a² + b² only when ab is positive
final_answer.spoken: thirty six x squared, plus sixty x, plus twenty five; the square of a sum is greater only when eigh b is positive

hold_back: 36x² + 60x + 25; (a + b)² is greater than a² + b² only when ab is positive
maths_rules: (a + b)² − (a² + b²) = 2ab, so (a + b)² is greater than a² + b² only when ab is positive
a = 5, b = −2: (5 + (−2))² = 9 but 25 + 4 = 29, so it is not always greater
check of the doubt: x = 1 gives (6 + 5)² = 121, and 36 + 25 = 61 is not 121
video_script.design: One idea: the square of a sum is the two squares plus twice the first times the second. Uses the cut square of the square of sixty five video. Wrong idea: square each term and add. The working stays on the board through the doubt.

narration: <bookmark mark='put'/>Step one, use the identity with eigh as six x and b as five.
<bookmark mark='sq'/>Six x squared is thirty six x squared.
<bookmark mark='mid'/>Twice six x times five is sixty x.
<bookmark mark='last'/>Five squared is twenty five.
That gives thirty six x squared, plus sixty x, plus twenty five.

beats.colours: the two thirty x pieces in one colour
narration: <bookmark mark='dist'/>Step two, expand by the distributive property instead.
Six x plus five, times six x plus five, gives four pieces.
<bookmark mark='four'/>They are thirty six x squared, thirty x, thirty x and twenty five.
<bookmark mark='same'/>Thirty x and thirty x make sixty x, and both ways agree.

<bookmark mark='left'/>That leftover is positive only when eigh b is positive.

narration: <bookmark mark='put'/>Step four, test eigh as five and b as negative two.
<bookmark mark='lhs'/>Eigh plus b is three, and three squared is nine.
<bookmark mark='rhs'/>But eigh squared plus b squared is twenty five plus four, which is twenty nine.
<bookmark mark='less'/>Nine is less than twenty nine, so the square of a sum is not always greater.

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks square each term and add, so the answer is thirty six x squared plus twenty five.
<bookmark mark='test'/>Test it with x as one. The question gives eleven squared, which is one hundred twenty one.
That answer gives only sixty one.
<bookmark mark='strike'/>The missing sixty x is the two strips of the square, so they must be added.
